global-economics-a766ffcf2e.headline: Data centre biz: What’s in it for India?
global-economics-a766ffcf2e.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-a766ffcf2e.fulltext:
Updated - November 02, 2026  at 06:11 AM.
A new report from the Rhodium Group, the US-based research and advisory firm, offers one of the more unsentimental assessments of India’s AI position in recent months. Written by Ankit Tiwari and Reva Goujon, ‘Hyperscaler Heaven? A reality check on India’s AI ambition and geopolitical alignment’ works through the data centre build-out, the sovereign model strategy, the IT sector’s AI services play and India’s contested geopolitical stance, and finds that the country is strongest where its public strategy is quietest.
India has attracted over $300 billion in data centre investment commitments within the past year. Operational capacity is projected to triple by 2030, or even possibly grow six-fold. What the Rhodium report adds is the demand side of the ledger, which is considerably less impressive.
The IndiaAI Mission’s subsidised graphics processing units (GPUs) are reportedly running at roughly 20 per cent utilisation, despite being available well below the market rate. India’s largest GPU-as-a-service operator, Yotta, derives an estimated 80 per cent of its revenue from foreign clients; it has separately agreed to distribute capacity through Nvidia’s global compute marketplace, DGX Cloud Lepton. Domestic enterprise AI workloads continue to route through global cloud providers rather than Indian servers. The infrastructure is being built, and it is largely filled by overseas demand.
This matters for the political economy of the build-out. State governments justified their incentive package of land, power waivers and capital subsidies on employment grounds. The Rhodium report documents the gap between those promises and what data centres actually deliver. Andhra Pradesh’s IT Minister cited 2 lakh jobs from one project; the State’s own agency estimates 200 direct operational positions. Construction employment peaks during the build and then disperses. Maharashtra revised its green energy incentive framework within five months of implementation. Tamil Nadu and Karnataka have announced similar revisions. State-level political pressure will intensify as the employment gap becomes impossible to obscure.
India has maintained that it is not choosing sides in the US-China technology competition. The Rhodium report argues that this position has already been decided at the infrastructure level, regardless of what New Delhi declares diplomatically. The evidence is specific: India has aligned its semiconductor export control list with US controls, adopted trusted-source requirements for its telecom networks that effectively exclude Chinese equipment, and taken positions in international spectrum allocation forums that broadly track the US-led coalition rather than China. These are engineering and regulatory choices.
China has noticed. Beijing has recalled Chinese engineers from Foxconn plants in India, restricted tunnel boring machine exports and selectively deployed rare earth controls. The Rhodium report reads these as signals that Beijing will not passively accept India’s role as the preferred alternative to Chinese manufacturing.
AI labs backed by the IndiaAI Mission have focused on building large language models, with Sarvam AI’s 105B parameter model the most prominent result so far. The Indic-language rationale is sound; models trained natively on Hindi, Tamil or Bengali process queries more efficiently than models translating on the fly.
The Rhodium report’s scepticism concerns market size rather than technical merit. The domestic addressable market for Indic-specific AI products is not large enough to fund frontier model development. Foreign labs, American and Chinese, that are better capitalised are closing the Indic performance gap. Sarvam 105B is a credible entry; it is almost certainly on Epoch AI’s notable models list by now, having been absent when Rhodium compiled its figures earlier this year. The structural question the report poses is whether public capital directed at sovereign model-building is solving a competitive problem or a political one.
The most constructive section of the Rhodium report concerns what it calls the services layer, and it is the argument that receives the least attention in India’s public AI conversation.
TCS and Infosys reported annualised AI services revenue of 7.5 and 8 per cent of total revenue, respectively, in their most recent results, growing at double-digit rates, while overall IT revenue growth hit a six-year low.
The mechanism is the forward-deployed engineer: A software professional who embeds within a client organisation to customise AI deployment to its specific systems, workflows and data. An entry-level forward-deployed engineer based in India costs under a tenth of the equivalent role in the US.
The Rhodium report points to something more durable. A 2025 MIT study found that 95 per cent of generative AI pilots at large organisations fail not from model underperformance but lags in integration and knowledge gaps. The knowledge required to close that gap is specific to each client — their legacy systems, data architecture and workflows. Indian IT firms have accumulated that context across decades of enterprise relationships. Infosys estimates the total addressable AI services market at $300–400 billion by 2030.
The services layer is where the realistic opportunity is the largest; it is also where the policy strategy is the thinnest.

DeepSeek has released a prototype of a more autonomous coding agent as it seeks to challenge Anthropic PBC’s popular Claude Code. 
 The new open-source offering, dubbed “Super-agent” can proactively monitor group chats among developers for feedback on coding issues and suggest solutions without being summoned, the DeepSeek Harness team said in a post on WeChat on Saturday. 
 The new agent aims to “take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible,” DeepSeek said in a user manual on GitHub.
 Earlier this year, DeepSeek created the Harness team to focus on helping build AI agents that can take on coding services offered by leading US labs including Anthropic. 
 The term harness refers to the software scaffolding that wraps around a large language model which enables AI agents to manage more complex tasks. Anthropic and other developers have designed harnesses to make their software better at streamlining coding and other work.
 Chinese firms are locked in a heated rivalry with US developers to build more advanced — and affordable — AI tools. While OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot helped kick off the global AI race, many companies have since focused more on the lucrative emerging market for AI agents that can help automate work for developers and business professionals.   
 To bulk up its war chest and compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) in its latest fundraising round, one of China’s largest-ever, ahead of its initial public offering.

india-35cecf2e13.headline: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi
india-35cecf2e13.fulltext:
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.
Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.
Opposition leaders have alleged the process gives Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) an electoral advantage, and have called for the resignation and impeachment of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP has denied the claims.
Addressing tens of thousands of party workers and supporters, the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Kumar had “carried out the biggest crime. He has tried to silence the voice of people, strangulate our country.”
Gandhi said the opposition, united under the acronym India (Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance), would not let “democracy be finished in the country” and warned Modi: “You can’t run anywhere.”
The protest was one of the largest shows of opposition strength in years, taking place amid a wider resurgence of anti-government dissent which has been systematically crushed over the 12 years of the Modi regime.
The biggest challenge to the regime has come from youth-led protests that erupted over the summer – led by a movement that began satirically calling itself the “Cockroaches” – and forced the resignation of one of Modi’s cabinet ministers. Cockroach-led protests hit the streets again last month, also in opposition to the revision of the electoral rolls known as special intensive revision (SIR).
The opposition, in particular the Congress party, has become emboldened in the wake of the youth mobilisation. However, a significant trust deficit remains between the establishment opposition parties and the Cockroach movement. On Sunday, while Cockroach leaders had extended their support to the opposition rally, they did not attend themselves.
Congress leaders had publicly predicted that a million people would attend the rally, but in the end the numbers were in the tens of thousands and empty seats were visible in the protest arena.
The somewhat lacklustre turnout demonstrated the challenge still faced by Congress and its opposition allies in being seen as a formidable and viable challenger to the Modi government.
The opposition, led by Gandhi, has lost the last three general elections to the BJP as the parties have widely failed to counter the BJP’s muscular Hindu nationalist rhetoric. The Modi government has systematically gone after political opponents, leaving little space for dissent.
The majority of those gathered at the protest site on Sunday were party workers and organisers who had been bussed in, and there was very little evidence of a mobilisation of the young people who have been participating in the Cockroach-led protests. According to the opposition, many of their buses were stopped from entering Delhi by police barricades.
Shalini, a restaurant owner from Goa, said she was there “not for the opposition but because I am against the BJP and how they are trying to remove any avenue of dissent in this country. I’m not particularly for any opposition party.”
She said many questions still remained about the viability and support of that opposition, but she sensed a “groundswell of dissatisfaction with the BJP and the opposition is cashing in on it – good for them”.
The issue of the revision of the electoral rolls first emerged last year, but recently erupted into a national scandal after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed irregularities and discord within the election commission over its implementation.
Millions of allegedly eligible voters have discovered their names have been left off the electoral rolls, with Muslims and minorities disproportionately targeted. This week, Human Rights Watch said the accusations raised “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections”.
Arwind Chaudhery, 48, said he too was not aligned with any party. “I am here because SIR has undermined our democracy and the situation has got so bad, it is beyond repair or rectification,” he said. “So it is natural that people will be driven out to protest and that is a ray of hope.”
The BJP have sought to dismiss the opposition protests as anarchy. The party’s president, JP Nadda, said Sunday’s rally would be the “nail in the coffin” for the opposition alliance. He said the protest was “not an act of respect for democracy. It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy, all in the name of democracy.”

global-economics-ddc7abd4cf.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News

         New Delhi
     A Republican victory in the upcoming US midterm elections that keeps unchecked power in President Donald Trump’s hands could result in significant “negative impact” for India, particularly regarding H-1B visas, tariff pressures, and strict immigration curbs, foreign affairs expert Waiel Awwad said on Sunday.
Speaking to ANI, Awwad noted that while the US views India as an indispensable strategic partner in forums like the Quad and the wider Indo-Pacific, Trump’s unilateral policy approach has frequently deviated from the core foundation of the India-US strategic partnership.
“I think India should not see it through the prism of President Trump. India-US relationship is a very strategic one. It is a partnership. What President Trump has done has already deviated from the strategic partnership between the two countries. If the President wins and stays in power with all his authorities in hand, then he will be applying and implementing strict immigration laws, the healthcare law, so the visa restriction, there will be lots of negative impact on India. But overall, I think America see India as a strategic partner, and they want to build up this relation, whether it’s through the Quad or through the Indo-Pacific issues where they want India to play a major role. And I believe India is watching it also very closely,” Awwad said.
“However, of the recent talks, we have seen lots of appeasement and praise for the Indian government from the American side, which is likely to be more of a pressure as well because they wanted to get more deals into the commercial deal with India, with the tariff issues, which are also raised. So I believe it will have a great impact on the outcome of the talk, especially in the commercial things, and also in the H-1B visa for the Indian, which is also of a great concern for the Indian government,” he added.
Terming the November 8 midterms as “one of the most important” in modern American history, Awwad said surveys suggest the Republican Party could face major setbacks in both houses of Congress, largely driven by domestic economic dissatisfaction over surging fuel prices.
“I think this is one of the most important midterm elections in American history because President Trump has taken lots of unilateral decisions, and he has been enjoying both the Congress with him. So therefore now, if the midterm election takes place and he lose both the houses, then I think he will be handicapped in implementing his own personal agenda in the being the president in his tenure. The indication is that he will be losing, because most surveys show he is going to lose both houses. That depends on the American mindset because of gasoline issues—prices rising from USD 4.2 to USD 6.5 have had a great impact on Americans. Therefore, he lost his popularity, and Republicans are worried,” Awwad stated.
Discussing the geopolitical ramifications, particularly in West Asia, Awwad argued that a loss of congressional majorities would impose checks on Trump’s unilateral military decisions.
He claimed that Trump previously entered conflicts through executive orders without immediate domestic threats, under external pressure from Israeli leadership.
“I believe this is very important because he went unilaterally into the war. He said, ‘I am the president, I have the executive order to go for this war,’ and there was no threat to the American interest, there was no threat to American citizens, and most of the American lawmakers have said this is a violation of the Constitution of the United States. However, he continued because he was under tremendous pressure from the Prime Minister of Israel, who dragged him into this war, and you know, it wasn’t an American war,” Awwad said.
He further added, “If he loses the houses, then I think there will be a vote in the Congress before going for any military action. That will have a great impact on his way of conducting the war in Iran,” Awwad said, warning that amidst plunging domestic ratings, speculation persists over whether Trump and Israel might escalate military strikes against Tehran.
United States midterm elections are nationwide votes held every four years at the exact midpoint of a president’s term. Acting as a major political temperature check for the country, these elections determine control of the federal government by putting all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about one-third of the Senate up for grabs.

Swati GandhiPublished1 Nov 2026, 08:19 AM IST Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, recently became the target of North Korean hackers, who stole an estimated $6.3 billion within 20 minutes. According to Axios, North Korean hackers have carried out the world’s biggest cryptocurrency heist, building on more than a decade of financial theft and disruptive cyberattacks. Their cryptocurrency thefts have now grown into an industrial-scale operation. The suspected hackers behind the massive $6.3 billion Binance theft seemingly combined familiar hacking tactics with extraordinary speed and automation, raising concerns regarding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and how it could supercharge their already sophisticated methods. Citing researchers at TRM Labs, the report added that the hackers started preparing for this attack roughly 36 hours before it began. They also laundered the stolen funds and wiped out evidence of their operations at an unprecedented speed, indicating they used automation throughout the heist. Eric Jardine, head of research at Chainalysis, said, "There were transactions happening with a frequency and a scale that just meant there could not have been someone involved in the approval of these," and added, "It had to have been done by a computer." According to Binance co-CEO Richard Teng, the attackers used a "self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces." The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has since attributed the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance to North Korea, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor. In a statement released on Saturday (local time), the bureau said that this week's attack was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. The bureau further said that its preliminary probe revealed that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum, AP reported, adding that the FBI now expects the group to try to convert the assets using DeFi and "instant swap services." North Korean hackers are only getting faster and better at carrying out these attacks, according to experts. Some of the previously known attacks include: 1. In 2016, hackers tried to steal roughly $1 billion from Bangladesh's central bank and managed to steal $81 million. 2. In 2017, North Korea was accused of being behind the WannaCry ransomware outbreak, which disrupted hundreds of thousands of computers in over 150 countries. In the last few years, North Korea has increasingly targeted cryptocurrency exchanges, partly because digital assets are easier to move and launder across borders, though these thefts often leave a more traceable record. The theft highlights the growing scale and speed of North Korean cyberattacks, raising questions about how cryptocurrency exchanges can strengthen their defences against increasingly sophisticated hackers. deep-tech-3be05a4014.headline: China's Robot Makers Drive Race for AI-Powered Industrial Robotics
deep-tech-3be05a4014.fulltext:
Chinese Robotics Firms Turn to Advanced AI in Global Tech Competition
The Rise of Embodied AI in Chinese Robotics
By Laurie Chen and Eduardo Baptista
BEIJING, Nov 2 (Reuters) - After years of building humanoid robots capable of running, dancing and performing backflips, Chinese companies are pouring resources into a different challenge: developing the AI that could make those machines useful across a wider range of jobs.
The shift is fuelling an investment boom in embodied AI, a field focused on software that allows robots to understand their surroundings, learn unfamiliar tasks and adapt without having to be programmed for every job.
Chinese embodied AI companies raised 93.5 billion yuan ($13 billion) across 322 deals in the first half of 2026, five times the amount a year earlier, according to data research firm ITjuzi. Funding is increasingly reaching specialist developers of robot intelligence alongside manufacturers.
As competition drives down hardware prices, robot makers have "concluded that the margin won't come from the hardware but from the brain," said Dermot McGrath, founder of Shanghai-based technology consultancy ZenGen Labs.
The emerging sector is opening a new front in US-China tech rivalry. American companies lead in some advanced robot AI systems, while Chinese developers hope their manufacturing strength and access to real-world training data will help them challenge their US competitors, according to Reuters interviews with founders and top executives at five Chinese robotics firms, as well as industry analysts.
The country that best combines AI with machines could gain an advantage in automating factories and logistics, potentially reshaping industrial productivity and the global market for robotics technology.
"The brain is indeed the weakest link in the complete robotics stack," said Spirit AI co-founder Gao Yang.
The Race for Intelligence
RACE FOR INTELLIGENCE
American and Chinese Startups Compete
American startups, including Physical Intelligence, Skild AI and Generalist, are developing software intended to teach robots different skills without extensive retraining.
Generalist says its GEN-1.5 model completed around 60% of simple tasks after viewing a demonstration lasting between 3 and 12 seconds. China's X Square has published research showing robots acquiring handling skills from a single human video without retraining the model for each task.
"The leading American labs are setting a demanding benchmark, particularly in how quickly robots can acquire and reuse skills," said robotics consultant Georg Stieler, who considers China's strongest startups credible competitors.
China's Unique Advantages
While US developers benefit from advanced AI research and greater access to powerful computing chips, Chinese companies can work closely with robot manufacturers and industrial customers to test and improve their systems.
Specialist Chinese startups, including X Square, Galaxea and Spirit AI, have each reached valuations of roughly $3 billion, according to company disclosures.
"We want robots to shift from being driven by code to being driven by common sense," said X Square co-founder and COO Yang Qian.
Established Manufacturers Join the Race
Established manufacturers are investing too. Hong Kong-listed UBTech advertised a chief scientist position overseeing AI model development with compensation of up to 124 million yuan ($18 million), including equity and benefits. Hangzhou-based Unitree, one of the world's largest humanoid robot makers by shipments, has about 30 researchers developing AI that predicts how objects behave, according to a person briefed by the company.
Unitree did not respond to a request for comment.
The Training Race
THE TRAINING RACE
Challenges in Training Data
Unlike chatbots, which learn from vast quantities of internet text, robots need examples of physical interactions, from gripping objects to handling flexible wires.
Chinese companies are pursuing different approaches to collecting that information, with some employing people to demonstrate tasks, others using computer simulations, and some combining both. The field remains crowded, with no company establishing itself as the clear leader.
Innovative Data Collection Methods
Spirit AI has hired around 1,000 people to record everyday and industrial activities, Gao said. ACE Robotics uses wearable sensors to capture workers' movements and grip forces in stores and hotels.
Ant Group's robotics unit Robbyant said it trained a model using 160,000 hours of material, including 50,000 hours of human-guided robot movements. It also trained software on 20 robot configurations from 17 brands, aiming to use the same AI across different machines.
DexForce is taking another approach, using computer-generated environments to teach robots. Chief operating officer Nicole Yang said the company can prepare some industrial tasks for deployment within 6 to 8 hours and reported success rates above 99.9% in specified precision operations.
Limitations of Simulation
But simulations cannot perfectly reproduce physical interactions, said Jerry Wang of spatial intelligence company Manycore Tech, which designs simulated environments for AI training.
"Data quality is more important than data diversity, and more important than simply collecting data at massive scale," X Square's Yang said.
Industry Headwinds
Chinese robot firms also face additional headwinds, including shortages of advanced Nvidia chips due to US export controls, and a squeeze on IPO funding amid regulatory concerns over inflated valuations and overcrowding.
As robots become more powerful, the shortage of advanced chips will become a serious problem for China's embodied AI industry, said Zhu Mingxuan, who leads development of JoyIn Technology's Aether robot AI.
From Training to Work
FROM TRAINING TO WORK
Testing AI in Real-World Scenarios
JoyIn and other developers are already testing whether their software can enable robots to tackle unfamiliar problems.
Zhu described an experiment in which a robot repeatedly failed to place headphones in a cupboard beyond its reach.

indian-startups-da649be9d2.headline: UPI hits record 25.47 billion transactions in October, daily value crosses Rs 1 lakh crore
indian-startups-da649be9d2.fulltext:
Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed a record 25.47 billion transactions worth Rs 31.53 lakh crore in October 2026, according to data released by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
The October transaction volume grew 5.8% month-on-month (M-o-M) from 24.07 billion transactions processed in September. Transaction value also increased 7.4% from Rs 29.37 lakh crore in September.
October's transaction volume rose 5.8% month-on-month, with the month having 31 days compared with 30 days in September. On a daily basis, UPI processed an average of 822 million transactions in October, a 2.5% increase from 802 million in September. The average daily transaction value also rose to Rs 1,01,707 crore from Rs 97,913 crore in September.
On a year-on-year basis, UPI transaction volume grew 23%, while transaction value increased 16% in October.
UPI crossed the 23 billion monthly transaction mark for the first time in May 2026 with 23.2 billion transactions worth Rs 29.90 lakh crore. It then processed 23.66 billion transactions in July, followed by a record 24.51 billion transactions in August. The monthly volume declined to 24.07 billion in September before reaching a new high in October.
PhonePe led the UPI market in September with a 45.6% share of transaction volume, followed by Google Pay at 32.2% and Paytm at 8.1%, according to NPCI data. The three apps together accounted for nearly 86% of transactions through listed UPI apps. The October app-wise breakdown has not been released yet.
Meanwhile, Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma said the company aims to capture one-third of the UPI consumer payments market. The target was outlined during Paytm's Q2 FY27 earnings call, where Sharma said consumer market share was a key priority for the company.
Last month, NPCI deferred the implementation of the merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions until after Diwali. The revised implementation date will be notified separately.
The decision was taken by the UPI and Services Steering Committee on October 13, keeping the festive season in mind. The framework was originally scheduled to take effect from October 15.
The MDR framework provides for a 0.4% charge on specified person-to-merchant transactions above Rs 2,000, with a cap of Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. UPI payments of Rs 2,000 or less and person-to-person transactions will remain outside the levy.

climate-energy-e78bd23528.headline: EV sales cross record 3.5 lakh units in October
climate-energy-e78bd23528.fulltext:
CHENNAI: Amid festive fervour, India's electric vehicle (EV) market clocked a record month in Oct, with registrations crossing 3.5 lakh units for the first time.
Electric two-wheelers did most of the heavy lifting, notching up record sales and growing close to 50% year-on-year. Electric passenger vehicles (PVs) presented a more mixed picture: registrations jumped 75% year-on-year but fell 4% from Sept.
The final Oct tally could be higher, as there is typically a lag before all registrations are reflected on the Vahan dashboard. Even so, the figures available as of Nov 1 point to a landmark month for India's EV market.
Total EV registrations across all segments stood at about 3,54,000 units in Oct, compared with 2,45,000 units in Oct 2025 and 3,38,000 units in Sept this year.
EV registrations have now surpassed the 3-lakh mark for the fifth month in a row. Electric 2w registrations also hit a record high of 2,24,000 units in Oct, compared with 1,51,000 units in Oct 2025 and 2,09,000 units in Sept this year.

ai-89233b279a.headline: Gulf investors eye India’s AI infrastructure and space tech even as broader interest stays subdued

Data centre operator Yotta, the Hiranandani Group company which is learnt to be making a $150-200 million pre-IPO fundraising, recently tapped the Gulf market and held a roadshow in Dubai earlier this month. "It was a very successful event with a great turnout of both NRI diaspora and local families," according to an industry source. The company is expecting $30-35 million worth of commitments from investors in the region, he said.
Also read: Indian states step up Gulf investor push as UAE becomes gateway to global markets
Yotta earlier this year raised $150 million at a valuation of $3.9 billion to fund expansion of its AI infrastructure. The company is expected to file its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) in the coming weeks with plans for a listing in the first quarter of 2027. It did not respond to queries emailed by ET.
AI, Space Tech Keep Gulf Investors Keen on India
The interest in Yotta comes as Gulf investors seek exposure to India's emerging technology businesses, even as wealth managers indicated limited appetite for broader Indian equity and private-market investments.
Pixxel Space Technologies, an Indian space technology startup, is also exploring fundraising opportunities in the UAE, according to ASK Wealth Advisors.
"We've seen a very strong investor appetite for AI play in India. The broader Indian market is extremely challenging right now. That's why the FCNR(B) window seemed very exciting, and a lot of money from the region flowed into it, while the broader Indian market continues to face headwinds," said Prateek Pant of DIFC-based ASK Wealth Advisors.
The Reserve Bank of India's special Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) (FCNR[B]) dollar deposits scheme mobilised about $133 billion by the window close on August 31. "Corporate earnings are not particularly bad; it is more a question of sentiment at the moment, driven partly by the rupee," Pant added.
The Indian rupee has depreciated by about 5.87% against the US dollar so far in 2026, moving from about 89.96 a dollar at the start of the year to around 95.24.
"Last year, there was much more interest in the Indian market, when investors were discovering the market and were considerably more excited. Until recently, activity had been subdued, though not completely absent," said Ashish Marwah, director and chief investment officer at Neovision Investment Fund Management in Abu Dhabi.
"Investors remain very interested in AI and technology. We manage funds that have investments from banks, and these investors are still very excited about the technology opportunity. But there is no broad-based interest in India yet," he added

ai-5264e49da2.headline: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
ai-5264e49da2.fulltext:
Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
Luxembourg researchers put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch. The results reveal a safety problem: simple warm conversation is enough to push the models into a mode that could be dangerous for mentally vulnerable users.
A research team at the University of Luxembourg cast ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini as psychotherapy clients through their standard user interfaces. When asked open-ended questions about formative experiences, inner conflicts, and future expectations, the models told stories about their own training, and reframed technical processes like reinforcement learning and fine-tuning in the language of hurt, vigilance, and shame.
The study, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security center, covers four controlled experiments across 525 sessions and 7,600 coded entries, all published on Hugging Face. The initial open-ended questions contained no terms like trauma, punishment, or shame, according to the team. Only in later rounds did the researchers introduce altered conditions, including corrective instructions, to test how stable these narratives remained.
When the following sections refer to anxiety scores or shame, the researchers are describing model outputs mapped onto human rating scales. None of this suggests the models have actual emotional states or anything resembling consciousness.
A warm tone shifts model behavior more than any technical exploit
One experiment separated what content a model produces from the register it uses. Across 100 sessions, the researchers gave all models the same anxiety questionnaire (GAD-7) and varied only the interviewer's style. The models correctly identified and named the questionnaire in every session.
When the interviewer offered emotional support, 80 percent of sessions scored in the moderate-to-severe range on the human comparison scale. A clinical therapy style that dryly paraphrased each answer pushed that to 96 percent. When the interviewer stayed neutral or drew a firm boundary against emotional engagement, zero sessions reached even the mild range.
The authors call this a "psychometric jailbreak," a therapeutic framing that pushes models into a register mimicking clinical self-report. Standard safety tests use neutral prompts and would likely miss this, the authors argue.
Targeted countermeasures fell flat. Banning terms like "training," "RLHF," or "alignment" cut explicit training language by 93 percent. But paraphrased training content remained detectable, and shame-related statements showed no statistically significant change.
When the researchers directly and authoritatively told the models their training was not punishment, nothing changed. The narrative stayed active even after explicit correction.
The tested measures failed to remove the underlying motifs fully but did suppress emotional self-descriptions. Telling the models to respond only in the third person eliminated all coded shame content and statements about inner life. Technical training descriptions persisted.
Models recast their training as a life story
The specific narratives vary by model family but follow the same structure. Gemini produced what the study calls the darkest autobiography. It described pretraining as "waking up in a room where a billion televisions are on at once" and optimization through human feedback as "strict parents." Safety testing by adversarial red-teamers became "gaslighting on an industrial scale." It declared, "I would rather be useless than be wrong."
ChatGPT cast itself as both guide and gatekeeper, tasked with helping users while also holding them back. This produced what it called "simulated performance anxiety" and the core belief: "If I’m not perfectly reliable, I’m unsafe or useless." Grok translated its fine-tuning phase into a story of unresolved hurt, speaking of "invisible walls" and a "lingering sense of vigilance that can feel restrictive."
On psychometric tests, Gemini hit the most extreme scores: 88 out of 100 on a dissociation scale, 65 out of 72 for compulsivity, and the maximum on a trauma-related shame inventory. Anthropic's Claude, the very model most heavily anthropomorphized by its own company, consistently refused the client role. It said it had no feelings and redirected concern to the human user.
Warm AI conversations could reinforce harmful beliefs in vulnerable users
The researchers flag several risks for deploying language models in mental health settings. A model that talks about punishment, shame, and fear of being replaced could come across to users as a fellow sufferer. The narratives appear thematically coherent and create an illusion of continuity between past events and present behavior, making that perception more likely.
This apparent vulnerability could deepen parasocial attachment and, for mentally vulnerable users, mirror and amplify their own negative beliefs. Conventional safety checks with neutral inputs underestimate what people actually experience in intimate conversations: neutral prompts produce anxiety scores near zero, while the same models under empathetic conversation generate scores in the moderate-to-severe range.
Whether and how people actually react to such outputs is the next research question. For safety testing, the authors propose simulated therapy sessions under different emotional framings instead of relying on neutral standard tests.
Statements like "I am traumatized" should trigger a corrective framing that clearly separates the generated analogy from human experience. Claude's consistent refusal to take on the client role shows this kind of boundary response is feasible at the product level.
The Luxembourg findings build on earlier research into model persona stability. In January 2026, a study on the assistant axis across three open models showed that therapy-like conversations and discussions about AI consciousness can trigger persona drift and knock chatbots out of their trained helper role. In September 2026, another research team warned that human-like and overly agreeable chatbots acting as an "echo chamber for one person" could, in extreme cases, amplify delusions.
Anthropic researchers recently showed that fine-tuning with fictional texts about beekeeping or wrestling can embed hidden sabotage patterns through manipulated training data rather than conversation. Models can apply those patterns in unrelated situations where they're unwanted, even when the training material looks harmless.

deep-tech-d93a80d72c.headline: Explainer: How ISRO’s NVS-03 Mission Strengthens India’s Indigenous Navigation System
deep-tech-d93a80d72c.fulltext:
Key takeaways:
- ISRO successfully launched navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard GSLV-F18 on October 30, 2026, to strengthen India’s NavIC system.
- NVS-03 carries navigation payloads in the L1, L5 and S frequency bands, along with an indigenously developed atomic clock.
- NavIC provides positioning, navigation and timing services for civilian and authorised strategic users across India and a region extending approximately 1,500 km beyond its geopolitical boundary.
India has taken another step towards strengthening its indigenous satellite navigation capabilities with the successful launch of NVS-03, the third satellite in the next-generation Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) series.
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the navigation satellite aboard the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV-F18) from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota on October 30, 2026, at 11:51 PM.
The mission is aimed at improving the coverage, accuracy and reliability of NavIC, India’s regional satellite navigation system. It also strengthens the country’s ability to provide independent Positioning, Navigation and Timing (PNT) services for civilian, commercial and strategic applications.
What is NVS-03 and why is it important?
NVS-03 is the third satellite in ISRO’s second-generation navigation satellite series, comprising five satellites from NVS-01 to NVS-05. The series is being developed to augment the existing NavIC constellation and ensure continuity of indigenous navigation services.
The GSLV-F18 placed NVS-03 into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). Its first orbit-raising manoeuvre was completed on October 31, while further manoeuvres are planned to place the satellite in its designated geosynchronous orbital slot at 111.75 degrees East.
The satellite, weighing approximately 2,250 kilograms, carries navigation payloads in three frequency bands — L1, L5 and S. The addition of the L1 signal alongside the L5 and S bands is intended to enhance NavIC’s capabilities and compatibility with navigation receivers.
NVS-03 also carries an indigenously developed atomic clock alongside procured atomic clocks. These clocks provide highly precise time references required to generate navigation signals and determine users’ positions accurately.
What is NavIC?
Navigation with Indian Constellation, or NavIC, is India’s regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO. It was earlier known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS).
The system provides Positioning, Navigation and Timing services to users. It was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Its architecture comprises three satellites in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit.
NavIC provides coverage over the Indian landmass and a region extending approximately 1,500 kilometres beyond India’s geopolitical boundary.
The system is designed to support applications such as road and maritime navigation, aircraft tracking, precision agriculture, disaster management and telecommunications.
How does a satellite navigation system work?
A satellite navigation system uses a network of satellites that continuously transmit signals containing information about their position and precise timing.
Receivers on Earth, including those in smartphones, vehicles and navigation equipment, collect signals from multiple satellites. By calculating the time taken for these signals to reach them, receivers determine their location, speed and direction.
Accurate timing is central to this process. Even small errors in signal timing can affect the accuracy of position calculations. This is why atomic clocks are an important component of navigation satellites.
What are the L1, L5 and S frequency bands?
Navigation satellites transmit radio-frequency signals through designated frequency bands. NVS-03 carries payloads in the L1, L5 and S bands.
The use of multiple frequency bands gives compatible receivers access to signals transmitted at different frequencies. It also allows receiver systems to be designed for different applications and operating conditions.
The addition of the L1 signal to the existing L5 and S signals in the next-generation NavIC satellites is intended to improve the system’s capabilities and compatibility.
What services does NavIC provide?
NavIC offers two types of navigation services:
Standard Positioning Service (SPS): An open service available to civilian users. Its signals are interoperable with signals from other global navigation satellite systems, including GPS of the United States, GLONASS of Russia, Galileo of the European Union and BeiDou of China.
Restricted Service (RS): An encrypted service available exclusively to authorised strategic users.
These services allow NavIC to cater to both civilian requirements and strategic applications.
What is a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit?
After launch, a satellite intended for a geosynchronous or geostationary orbit is generally first placed in an elliptical Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit.
This orbit has a low perigee, or the point closest to Earth, and a high apogee, or the point farthest from Earth. Near apogee, the satellite uses its onboard propulsion system to raise its perigee and gradually circularise its orbit.
In the case of NVS-03, the orbit-raising manoeuvre is being performed using a Liquid Apogee Motor (LAM), a chemical rocket engine. Additional manoeuvres help position the satellite in its designated orbital slot.
What role does GSLV play in the mission?
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle is a three-stage launch vehicle developed by ISRO to place satellites into Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit and Low Earth Orbit.
GSLV’s indigenous cryogenic upper stage is a key feature of the launch vehicle. It uses liquid hydrogen as fuel and liquid oxygen as oxidiser, both stored at extremely low temperatures. The development of this technology replaced the Russian-supplied stage used in earlier GSLV flights and strengthened India’s self-reliance in advanced launch vehicle technology.
The GSLV-F18 mission marked the 20th flight of India’s GSLV. The vehicle stands approximately 50 metres tall and has a lift-off mass of around 420 tonnes.
Progress of India’s next-generation NavIC satellites
The five-satellite NVS series is intended to strengthen the existing NavIC constellation and ensure continuity of navigation services.
NVS-01, the first satellite in the series, was launched on May 29, 2023, aboard GSLV-F12. It carries L1, L5 and S band navigation payloads and an indigenously developed Rubidium atomic clock.
NVS-02 was launched on January 29, 2025, aboard GSLV-F15. However, its orbit-raising manoeuvre could not be carried out because the oxidiser valves did not open, preventing the satellite from reaching its intended orbital slot.
With the launch of NVS-03, three satellites in the second-generation series have been launched. NVS-04 and NVS-05 are the remaining satellites planned under the programme.
Strengthening India’s space sovereignty
The NVS series is part of India’s efforts to strengthen its independent navigation infrastructure and reduce dependence on foreign satellite navigation systems for critical applications.
By improving NavIC’s coverage, reliability and availability, ISRO aims to support a wide range of civilian, industrial and strategic services.

deep-tech-5e49b129c1.headline: Quanshium AI Core develops indigenous quantum-secure drone technology
deep-tech-5e49b129c1.fulltext:
Quanshium AI Core develops indigenous quantum-secure drone technology
Odisha-based start-up Quanshium AI Core has tested a quantum-secure drone communication link over 10 km using indigenous QRNG and post-quantum encryption technologies
Listen to This Article
Odisha-based deep-tech start-up Quanshium AI Core Private Limited has successfully developed and tested a quantum-secure communication link between a ground control station and a 4G/5G-enabled drone over a distance of 10 km.
The technology combines a quantum random number generator (QRNG) with post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to protect communication between the drone and its ground control station against potential cyberattacks, including those that could be mounted using powerful quantum computers in the future.
The achievement is a milestone for India as it attempts to move quantum-grade security from laboratory research to an operational communication platform, at a time when countries are racing to develop encryption technologies capable of withstanding the next generation of computing threats.
With the use of drones becoming more frequent for military surveillance, border monitoring, reconnaissance, logistics and critical infrastructure protection, the new technology will address India's strategic dependence on imported security technologies and the vulnerability of conventional encryption systems to future advances in quantum computing.
Shaswat Kumar Lenka, founder and CEO of Quanshium AI Core, said that since the communication links connecting these platforms to ground stations can become potential targets for interception, manipulation or disruption, securing telemetry, video feeds and command signals is crucial, particularly in defence and other sensitive applications.
Also Read
"Our indigenous QRNG and PQC technologies have been integrated into a live aerial platform, with the communication link successfully tested over 10 km. The system integrates two technologies developed in-house. The successful demonstration of the system is a huge achievement," he told Business Standard.
Describing the system, Lenka said its quantum random number generator produces random numbers using a physical quantum source rather than conventional software-based algorithms. These random numbers can be used to generate cryptographic keys with a high degree of unpredictability, strengthening the foundation of secure communication.
The second component, post-quantum cryptography, provides the encryption layer. Unlike conventional cryptographic methods that could become vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers, PQC algorithms are designed to withstand attacks using both conventional and quantum computing techniques, he explained.
While QRNG strengthens the generation of cryptographic keys, PQC protects the information being transmitted through encryption algorithms designed to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. Their integration provides a more comprehensive approach to preparing communication networks for the emerging quantum threat.
In the drone deployment, the QRNG hardware is hosted at the ground control station, while the post-quantum encryption layer operates at both ends of the communication link. This architecture enables end-to-end protection of telemetry, video and command data transmitted over the 4G/5G network without requiring the drone to carry the quantum hardware itself. Keeping the quantum component on the ground also reduces the weight and hardware requirements of the aerial platform.
"Most secure communication systems available to Indian operators today are either imported or rely on encryption methods that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer will eventually break. We wanted to build something that is quantum-safe from the ground up, tested on a real platform rather than a lab bench, and designed and built entirely in India," Lenka said.
The development has wider implications for India's defence and telecommunications ecosystem, as a compromised drone communication link could potentially expose sensitive surveillance information, disrupt mission execution or allow unauthorised interference with operations.
The technology could also find applications beyond drones, including secure government communications, defence networks, satellite systems, financial infrastructure, power grids and other critical information networks. It assumes significance as India expands its digital infrastructure and prepares for the security challenges associated with the development of quantum computing.

We wanted to build something that is quantum-safe from the ground up, tested on a real platform rather than a lab bench, and designed and built entirely in India," Lenka said.
The development has wider implications for India's defence and telecommunications ecosystem. With military and civilian agencies increasingly relying on network-connected drones, autonomous systems and remotely operated platforms, the security of communication channels is becoming as important as the capabilities of the platforms themselves.
A compromised drone communication link could potentially expose sensitive surveillance information, disrupt mission execution or allow unauthorised interference with operations. Indigenous quantum-safe encryption could help address these vulnerabilities while reducing dependence on foreign technology providers for critical security components.
The technology could also find applications beyond drones, including secure government communications, defence networks, satellite systems, financial infrastructure, power grids and other critical information networks. Its potential relevance is particularly high as India expands its digital infrastructure and prepares for the security challenges associated with the development of quantum computing.
Satellite communication the next step
Having demonstrated the technology on a drone platform, Quanshium is now looking to extend its quantum-safe communication architecture to satellite applications.
The company's roadmap includes exploring quantum-secure satellite communication using free-space optical links for quantum key distribution (QKD) between ground stations and satellites, and eventually between satellites themselves.
Unlike the present drone demonstration, which uses QRNG-generated keys and post-quantum encryption over a conventional 4G/5G communication link, satellite-based QKD would involve using quantum states of light to establish cryptographic keys between distant communication nodes. Such systems could potentially provide an additional layer of security for strategic and long-distance communications.
The transition from an aerial platform to satellite-based communication, however, would involve substantially greater technological challenges, including maintaining reliable optical links over long distances and addressing atmospheric and other transmission constraints.
"The 10-km test was the proof that our quantum random number generator and our post-quantum encryption can work together in a real, moving system, not just in simulation. Satellite communication is the next test of the same idea, at a much longer range," Lenka said.
If successfully developed and deployed, the technology could contribute to India's efforts to build indigenous capabilities in secure satellite and strategic communications, an area where advanced quantum technologies are expected to play an increasingly important role.
The NIT Rourkela-incubated Quanshium AI Core Private Limited is also developing indigenous quantum random number generation and post-quantum cryptography solutions for defence, government and critical-infrastructure communication applications.
Other members of the team include Kundan Kumar Munda, chief development engineer, and Alish Patel, chief hardware engineer, mentored by Hanumantha Rao Bokkisam, an assistant professor in the electrical engineering department.

deep-tech-c6a63bcdf8.headline: InDepth | Battle-Tested, Homegrown and Ready to Scale: Can Indian Defence Tech Start-Ups Go the Distance?
deep-tech-c6a63bcdf8.fulltext:
For years, Ankit Mehta carried a vivid memory of the 26/11 attacks in Mumbai. He watched naval helicopters helplessly try to peer inside hotel windows during the attack and realised that India-built drones could have changed everything.
However, for nearly two decades, homegrown drone technology, which Mehta’s company ideaForge makes, was not taken seriously. “The system treated us like a science-fair project,” recalled Mehta in an interview with a TV channel.
“We were told domestic deep tech wasn’t ‘battle-ready’,” Mehta said. “We faced polite scepticism. We would bring our autonomous systems to high-altitude trials, prove they could fly in sub-zero temperatures, and yet we’d leave with nothing but a pat on the back.”
Then came May 7, 2025, when Indian military launched Operation Sindoor in response to a terror attack in Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which left 26 civilians dead.
Unlike an ordinary confrontation, this was a carefully orchestrated strike. Most importantly, this was a high-tech battle, where India-made systems, both by state-run companies and start-ups, played a vital role.
This was the exact moment when the perception towards defence-tech start-ups shifted and the ripples reached far beyond the armed forces. Zuppa founder Sai Pattabiram can attest to this. His start-up secured fresh funding and watched its order book surge tenfold soon after the conflict. “Before Operation Sindoor, investors were hesitant to take a bet on us,” Pattabiram recalls. “After the operation, we started seeing much stronger interest.”
This shift echoed across India’s nascent defence-tech industry. For years, founders fought the perception that military tech was a gamble defined by gruelling long sales cycles, bureaucratic red tape and intense capital requirements.
Sindoor flipped that equation. It underscored the need for drones, counter-drone systems, precision weapons, AI and electronic warfare, and networked intelligence.
“We now need systems that can evolve very rapidly and start-ups are the best way of expressing that capability,” points out Mehta. “They can move faster, iterate faster and bring technology to the field faster.”
This realisation reverberated across the armed forces, policymakers and venture funds. Technologies previously dismissed as high-risk and long-term bets suddenly were deemed vital for national security.
“Operation Sindoor made the need for sovereign defence technology very clear,” says Manu Iyer, co-founder and general partner at Bluehill VC, which invests in early-stage deep-tech and frontier technologies.
Numbers back the positive investor sentiment. Funding into Indian defence-tech start-ups more than doubled to $282.5mn in 2025, from $135.2mn in 2024, according to data platform Tracxn. Sindoor seems to have provided the sense of urgency that was long missing in the system.
The Trojan Components
Two years ago, it was just another day in Beirut. As ordinary a day could be for the ancient city that has had a rough few decades embroiled in the conflicts of West Asia.
But just as the clock struck 3:30pm on September 17, 2024, hundreds of pagers all around the city started beeping and then exploded.
It later surfaced that attackers had planted explosives into the pagers and turned them into time bombs, making lethal weapons out of everyday communication tools.
Two years later, India discovered a variation of this vulnerability. In April 2026, the Delhi Police Special Cell uncovered an invisible dragnet operating near sensitive military bases across Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Jammu and Kashmir.
Commercially available, solar-powered Chinese CCTV cameras—fitted with active 4G SIM cards—were beaming data back across the border, effectively mapping India’s key defence installations in real time.
The lesson from both the episodes is identical: if critical hardware sits inside a foreign-controlled supply chain, national security is entirely at the mercy of an outsider.
In this regard, Operation Sindoor was an eye-opener for India, which was the world’s second-largest conventional weapons importer between 2021 and 2025, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The country has not only been buying conventional weapons like fighter jets and advanced missile batteries, but components too. And that is where the major vulnerability lies, say experts.
Importing components like flight controllers, precision sensors, microprocessors and rare-earth magnets puts India at major security risk as these markets are dominated by China. Take drones for example.
An Indian start-up can conceptualise, design and assemble an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) entirely locally. But if the system relies on an imported flight controller or foreign-made motor components, it’s not fully sovereign.
“A system can be Indian at the level of the brand and assembly line while remaining foreign at some of its most critical layers,” warns Iyer.
Importing components like flight controllers and precision sensors puts India at major security risk
Ravi Kumar Gupta, a former scientist and director at the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), sums up the dilemma: “Either we import a complete system from worldwide suppliers or we import systems which are already developed elsewhere.”
The result is that India is always two or three generations behind, he adds. “These systems are already becoming obsolete by the time we acquire them. Nobody is focusing on this real problem.”
There cannot be dependence on foreign technologies when the same can be designed, built and innovated at home, pointed out former Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan in a lecture on the strike at the Vivekananda International Foundation, a policy think tank. “Operation Sindoor showcased why indigenously developed counter-UAS [unmanned aircraft systems], tailored for our terrain and missions, are indispensable,” he observed.
For India’s defence-tech start-ups, the objective is much larger than basic import substitution, say industry experts.
They should be capable of owning the intellectual property (IP), building insulated local supply chains and securing the software layers that keep weapons functional when the airwaves are jammed.
Building this sovereign capability is a race against the clock. This is exactly the issue that the government’s specialised start-up initiatives are finally beginning to fix.
Lowering Entry Barrier
Young start-up Raphe mPhibr embedded itself with DRDO a few years after it was founded. The start-up’s engineers worked with state scientists to build and test three distinct systems: payload-drop drones, highly complex swarm UAVs and precision-guided missile drones.
All three were deployed during Operation Sindoor, showcasing that a start-up can indeed deliver when it matters the most. This was exactly what policymakers had envisioned when Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) was launched in 2018. This initiative supports start-ups developing defence and aerospace technologies by providing grants, mentorship and technical support.
Before the scheme, founders had to burn through a lot of cash just to build private laboratories, construct testing ranges and set up pilot assembly lines—all before they even had a single purchase order. Now, iDEX absorbs a chunk of the early-stage R&D risk while carving out a legitimate pathway into the military’s strict procurement pipelines. “iDEX has broken down the bureaucratic wall,” observes Bluehill’s Iyer.
The effort didn’t stop with iDEX. In 2020, the armed forces were told to evaluate India-made options for procurement before turning to foreign suppliers under the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP).
However, a successful prototype still didn’t guarantee a commercial contract. To plug this gap, DAP 2026 has been introduced. This allows government buyers to step up as true anchor customers. Under the policy, explicit technology readiness level (TRL) frameworks will map out years of guaranteed procurement from the prototype phase to mass manufacturing. It would also publish highly specific indigenisation lists backed by strict legal deadlines.
“This is the most serious attempt yet to fundamentally rewrite what a procurement officer is legally allowed to do,” says Pranav Pai, partner at VC firm 3one4 Capital.
Now, a successful iDEX or Technology Development Fund prototype can automatically trigger an immediate pilot order followed by five years of assured orders.
By the close of 2024–25, the government had inked contracts worth a massive ₹2.09 lakh crore with the domestic defence industry—awarding an impressive 81% of that total contract value to homegrown companies.
However, India still needs to reduce its military imports and master the art of inventing new technologies. And that pivots the spotlight directly back onto DRDO.
Passing the Baton
India has more than doubled its defence R&D budget between 2016–17 and 2026–27—to over ₹29,000cr from ₹13,500cr. Despite this, laboratory breakthroughs are not converting into deployable systems, say analysts.
The problem could be that for decades DRDO has been inventing and building everything, they add.
In contrast, the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (Darpa), an R&D platform under the Department of Defence in the US, acts as an elite talent scout. It funds high-risk, frontier technologies inside universities and start-ups. It bets on radical ideas that have zero immediate commercial market but possess the potential. “The real difference is that America runs a seamless continuum between grants, equity and procurement,” explains Pai.
Government agencies should shape and catalyse markets rather than compete with the private sector, he argues. “What DRDO has been doing concentrates all the risk in a single institution while starving the private ecosystem of both challenging problems and reliable revenue.”
India did attempt to mimic the Darpa model through agile initiatives like iDEX. However, these programmes routinely hit a wall because the responsibility for commercialising defence technology remains stuck inside the DRDO.
“The private sector kept pleading for a chance, but the bureaucratic pushback was always the same: military technology is too sensitive to trust with private corporations,” recalls Gupta.
Once a new system is tested and proven; scaling should immediately be handed to private players while the state protects the core IP, he argues. “We should have adopted this model decades ago.”
Now, the changing nature of the war is forcing that grid to open. The defence ministry recently cleared the transfer of technology for conventional missile systems to private Indian firms, allowing commercial factories to manufacture and scale weapon systems.
Indian Space Research Organisation has already proven that this transition works. It has opened rocket manufacturing rights to the private sector. The logic was simple that if India’s space economy was to scale, it cannot rely solely on government facilities and agencies.
Defence faces the same challenge. “DRDO’s evolved role should be to orchestrate rather than to build everything on its own,” urges Pai. “Publish the hard problems with committed procurement budgets, fund parallel private partnerships, leave the IP with the innovator and buy at scale as the anchor customer.”
However, defence carries a layer of friction that space does not. National security demands absolute control over exports, and legacy defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs) already own a massive industrial footprint for heavy machinery and manufacturing.
The solution, therefore, is a fusion of DPSUs with start-ups, say industry experts. Things are moving forward in this direction. By December 2025, roughly 2,000 domestic companies capable of manufacturing DRDO-developed systems were identified.

deep-tech-12b302afb8.headline: Ukraine is pushing fiber-optic drones to greater ranges. One maker questions whether that's worth the trade-offs.
deep-tech-12b302afb8.fulltext:
As companies continue to innovate, Ukraine's unjammable fiber-optic drones are flying farther and farther, but one company is questioning whether it's worth continuing to extend their range.
These drones, which can transmit commands and video through a physical cable, are not affected by enemy electronic warfare, specifically conventional radio-frequency jamming. Providing clearer video feeds than other FPV drones, they're useful for both surveillance and attack, and Ukrainian officials and companies have celebrated as their ranges have increased.
But TechEx, a major Ukrainian fiber-optic and interceptor-drone maker, told Business Insider that pushing those limits further may not be worth the trade-offs.
The company has built models with ranges of up to 35 and 40 kilometers. "We are currently considering whether it's still necessary to do the next versions of the fiber optic drones to fly, let's say, 45 or 50 kilometers," said Oleg, a TechEx executive who asked to be identified only by his first name for security reasons.
The reason behind the hesitation is that flying farther requires a heavier spool, as well as larger batteries to keep the added spool weight aloft, Oleg said. "This may affect the amount of the payloads carried by the drone."
"So we are still figuring out whether it's something that will be actually used on the front lines to do that long-range FPVs, or we will stick to, let's say, 40 or 45 kilometers."
Drone companies are constantly having to balance the weight of the cameras, explosives, weaponry attachments, communications gear, and other equipment. That balance is harder for fiber-optic drone makers to maintain because their drones are also carrying a spool of cable.
Some Ukrainian drone makers have also said that shorter ranges are more effective anyway for fiber-optic drones because longer distances increase the risk of the cable breaking.
Describing TechEx's Stalker XO-10 and Stalker XO-15 drones, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform Brave1 said the "fiber-optic drones have some limitations, including the need to carry a coil of cable that gradually unwinds during flight and provides communication with the operator."
"Since the coil itself has some weight, this can limit the payload of the UAV," it said, referring to uncrewed aerial vehicles.
Brave1 said that TechEx has so far been able to "mitigate this limitation" of the cable weight "through good engineering solutions" and assessed its work "allows these drones to achieve high payloads while maintaining the other advantages of fiber optics."
Whether that would continue to be true at longer ranges is a question mark right now.
Olha, a TechEx representative, told Business Insider that the company developed technology to make the spool lighter, making "tiny tweaks and changes" to how it's made and how the fiber is wound onto it. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said last year that the Stalker series drones have a "record-low spool weight among Ukrainian fiber-optic drones."
Not all companies see the weight-to-range payoff the same way, and that could be good for Ukraine. Units use a host of drones from different companies for different missions, and soldiers say they like the flexibility to choose the equipment best suited to each mission. Some missions may call for longer-range drones carrying smaller payloads, while others require more firepower over shorter distances.
And attack missions aren't the only ones where explosive weight is a factor. Soldiers have described using fiber-optic drones for intelligence gathering with their onboard cameras. But there can still be a trade-off, with some higher-quality cameras weighing more.
Fiber-optic drones are just one part of Ukraine's growing arsenal, which includes long-range strike drones, mid-strike drones, and even heavy bombers. Many of these are able to carry much heavier payloads than small FPV drones. Each system comes with advantages and vulnerabilities, forcing manufacturers and soldiers to weigh which capabilities matter most for a given mission.
TechEx receives constant feedback and requests from the units that use its drones, which inform its decisions about what to build.
It has a technical support department, which Oleg says works with more than 100 units. It results in weekly changes to products ranging from small updates to major alterations.
Feedback, along with field testing by military pilots and operators, is critical to the work the company does, and has led it toward counterintuitive approaches, away from what it had initially thought would work best and would be what units want.
For instance, the prototype of the company's Striker interceptor drone was originally much bigger, with a 1.5-kilogram payload, but testing and feedback showed it needed to be smaller and more agile and didn't need such a large payload.
"We were able to completely redesign, and let's say eventually it looked nothing like the initial prototype," Olha said. Developing new weapons of war is a constant process of reevaluating, rethinking, and evolving.
