indian-startups-86ff11ebf5.headline: Meesho’s Next Monetisation Engines
indian-startups-86ff11ebf5.fulltext: Meesho has spent much of its journey building scale in India’s value commerce market. Its low-cost marketplace model has helped it expand its reach beyond large cities, bring more sellers online and attract consumers looking for affordable products. But as the company moves towards its next phase of growth, the goalpost is shifting from acquiring users and expanding transactions to extracting more value from the ecosystem it has built. Advertising is emerging as one of the key opportunities. With 284 Mn annual transacting users (ATUs) and 1.13 Mn annual transacting sellers as of Q2 FY27, Meesho has a large marketplace that it can potentially monetise through sponsored listings and other advertising products. The company expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor to its revenue mix from FY28. At the same time, Meesho is exploring newer business lines, including lending products for consumers and sellers, while expanding branded commerce through Meesho Mall and discovery-led shopping through content commerce. These initiatives could open up additional revenue streams, although their contribution to the company's financials remains at an early stage. The opportunity comes as Meesho makes progress on its marketplace economics. Its Q2 FY27 performance shows that the core marketplace is growing and its operating economics are improving. Revenue from operations increased 34% year-on-year to ₹4,119.9 Cr, while net merchandise value (NMV) grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr. In the reported quarter, its contribution margin improved to 6% of net merchandise value (NMV), compared with 4.6% in the previous quarter and 3.3% a year earlier. Its marketplace adjusted EBITDA loss also narrowed to ₹130.5 Cr from ₹371 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, management cautioned that the 6% contribution margin recorded in Q2 FY27 should not be viewed as the new normal, as some of the logistics efficiency gains may be passed on to consumers and sellers to support growth. The question, therefore, is whether Meesho can turn its growing consumer and seller base into higher-value revenue streams without compromising the affordability that underpins its marketplace. Advertising: Can Meesho Monetise Its Scale? Advertising offers Meesho a way to generate more revenue from the traffic and transactions already flowing through its platform. As its user base and seller ecosystem expand, the company has an opportunity to charge sellers for better visibility and access to consumers who are actively browsing products. For sellers, sponsored placements can help products stand out in a crowded marketplace. For Meesho, they can create an additional revenue stream without requiring it to take ownership of inventory or significantly change its core marketplace model. This is particularly relevant in a business where affordability and low prices remain central to customer acquisition. The scale of the opportunity is supported by Meesho's operating metrics. Its ATUs grew 21% year-on-year to 284 Mn in Q2 FY27, while annual transacting sellers increased 60% to 1.13 Mn. Placed orders rose 17% to 819 Mn during the quarter, and NMV grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr. “A larger marketplace gives Meesho more opportunities to connect seller advertising with consumer discovery. However, the size of its user base alone does not determine how much it can earn from ads. The company will need to demonstrate that sellers are willing to spend consistently on advertising and that paid placements generate measurable returns through product views and orders,” an ecommerce analyst said. Advertising monetisation is still at a relatively early stage. On the Q2 FY27 earnings call, it said the sequential improvement in contribution margin was primarily driven by logistics efficiencies, rather than a significant increase in advertising monetisation. It also expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor as a percentage of NMV in FY28. Motilal Oswal expects higher advertising monetisation to support contribution margin expansion from FY28, citing seller demand for advertising and the potential to improve the platform's monetisation. However, Meesho will have to balance monetisation with the shopping experience. Its value-commerce positioning depends on offering consumers affordable products and a wide selection. If sponsored placements make discovery less relevant or push sellers towards higher advertising expenditure that is eventually reflected in product prices, the company could risk weakening some of the advantages of its model. The other consideration is the distribution of advertising benefits across sellers. Larger and more established sellers may have greater capacity to spend on visibility, while smaller sellers could find it harder to compete for prominent placements. Meesho will need to build an advertising ecosystem that delivers returns for sellers across different sizes and categories, the analyst added.. The key monitorable, therefore, is not simply the growth in advertising revenue, but how much of that revenue Meesho can retain as incremental contribution after accounting for the cost of serving the marketplace. If advertising can scale without materially increasing operating costs or affecting affordability, it could become a more durable margin lever. New Initiatives: Lending, Mall And Content Commerce Beyond advertising, Meesho is looking to deepen its engagement with consumers and sellers through a wider set of services. These initiatives could increase the number of ways in which the company earns from its ecosystem, although they are at different stages of development. One area is lending. During the earnings call, management confirmed that Meesho is working on both consumer-side and seller-side lending products. The company is expanding its network of non-banking financial company (NBFC) partners and is also looking to work with banks. For consumers, access to credit could potentially support purchases on the platform, while seller financing could help merchants manage working capital and grow their businesses. If structured effectively, these offerings could strengthen Meesho's relationship with both sides of the marketplace. However, the company has not disclosed lending-related assets under management, revenue targets or the expected financial contribution of these products. It is also not clear how much of the lending opportunity Meesho intends to capture directly versus through its lending partners. For now, it is better viewed as an emerging business opportunity than an established monetisation engine. Meesho Mall and content commerce represent another route to deepen marketplace engagement. Meesho Mall, which had around 1,800 brands in Q2 FY27, recorded 81% YoY growth in NMV. NMV from Tier 3 and smaller markets grew 89%, while around half of Mall customers during the quarter were first-time buyers on the branded-commerce offering. The growth indicates that Meesho is making progress in bringing branded products to a consumer base that has traditionally been associated with unbranded and lower-priced merchandise. A broader product mix could help the platform attract new customer segments and increase the range of purchases made by existing users. Content commerce is also expanding. Its NMV grew 160% YoY in Q2 FY27, while the number of content pieces generating orders increased 144% to 2.2 Mn. The ecosystem had more than 4 lakh sellers participating in content-led commerce. The proposition is to use videos and other content formats to help consumers discover products, rather than relying entirely on search-led shopping. This could create more product discovery opportunities and potentially improve engagement. Meesho has also said that the share of orders coming from discovery-led recommendations has increased, alongside time spent on the platform. However, rapid growth from these offerings does not automatically translate into a meaningful revenue contribution. Meesho has not disclosed the share of total NMV generated by Mall or Content Commerce, nor has it provided specific monetisation targets for either. Their longer-term value will depend on whether they can increase purchase frequency, attract higher-value transactions and create additional opportunities for advertising. AI is another part of this effort. Meesho is using AI across product discovery, ranking, fraud prevention and logistics, while also deploying AI agents in engineering and other internal functions. The company said 65% of its engineering pods were operating with one engineer directing AI agents. It reported a 41% reduction in code-review approval time and a reduction in data-science model deployment time from 17 days to three days. These productivity gains could help the company develop products and improve operations faster. But AI also brings infrastructure costs. Meesho's GPU footprint increased 150%, while server costs rose to 2.3% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 1.9% in the previous quarter. Management expects these costs to normalise towards the previous baseline as a percentage of NMV by Q4 FY27, but that remains an expectation to be tested. The newer initiatives are also still investment-heavy. Management has indicated that it is keeping investments in these businesses within a cap of around ₹200 Cr, while emphasising that product-market fit and unit economics will be important before scaling further. This suggests that Meesho is not yet positioning these offerings as immediate contributors to profitability. The Profitability Test The monetisation opportunity has to be seen alongside Meesho's broader effort to improve its marketplace economics. The company reported a contribution margin of ₹775 Cr in Q2 FY27, up from ₹531 Cr in Q1 FY27. As a percentage of NMV, the margin improved to 6% from 4.6% sequentially. The improvement was largely driven by lower logistics costs, supported by better order density, network redesign, improved route utilisation and efforts to reduce return-to-origin (RTO) orders. Management also indicated that it intends to recover some of the logistics-related margin spread lost in FY26 towards FY25 levels during FY27. However, it has cautioned against extrapolating the Q2 contribution margin as the new normal. Some of the savings could be passed on to sellers and consumers through lower prices, while a part may be retained to improve profitability. The timing and extent of this balance will matter as Meesho enters the festive period and continues to invest in growth. There are also costs that could absorb some of the gains. Meesho's advertising and sales promotion expenses increased ahead of the festive season, taking growth spending to 2.9% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 2.1% in Q1. Server costs also rose, reflecting the higher computing requirements of the platform. The company reported a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹172.1 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹132.4 Cr from ₹411.4 Cr a year earlier. Although the marketplace business is moving towards better unit economics, its newer initiatives continue to add to the overall loss. Cash flow also needs to be viewed over a longer period. Meesho reported positive consolidated free cash flow of ₹345 Cr in Q2 FY27, compared with an outflow of ₹226 Cr in Q1. But its last-twelve-month consolidated free cash flow remained negative at ₹565 Cr. The quarterly improvement was partly supported by seasonal working-capital movements, as collections from consumers ahead of the festive sale preceded settlements with sellers. This makes the quality and durability of cash generation an important measure of progress. Advertising could help improve margins because it allows Meesho to monetise marketplace activity without taking on inventory. climate-energy-3f2de85a2b.headline: India’s Solar Manufacturing Capacity Boom Faces a Cell Supply Gap
climate-energy-3f2de85a2b.fulltext:
Solex Energy’s plan to build solar module and cell manufacturing capacity in the United States is more than an overseas expansion proposal. It also highlights a structural imbalance within India’s renewable-energy supply chain: the country has reported module manufacturing capacity of about 262 GW, but cell capacity of only around 37 GW as of October 2026.
The Gujarat-based company is considering US investments as part of a $1.5 billion roadmap through 2030, according to Chairman and Managing Director Chetan Shah. The company currently operates a 4 GW module manufacturing facility in Gujarat and plans to raise its module capacity to 10 GW. It is also establishing 10 GW of cell manufacturing capacity and 2 GW of ingot and wafer production.
The proposed US facilities have not yet been detailed. Shah told PTI that the company is studying possible locations, investment requirements and other parameters. He did not disclose project specifics, citing regulatory compliance. The immediate announcement, therefore, is not a confirmed construction schedule or a finalised investment commitment in the US. It is an expansion plan being evaluated within a larger corporate investment programme.
Its significance lies in the supply-chain choices behind solar deployment. Solar modules are assembled from cells, while cells depend on upstream inputs such as wafers and ingots. A large module-making base without a comparable cell-manufacturing ecosystem can leave manufacturers dependent on limited domestic supplies or imports. Shah’s comments place that imbalance at the centre of the company’s argument for expanding across more stages of production.
The mismatch is considerable on the figures cited by the company chairman. India’s reported module manufacturing capacity is about seven times its cell capacity. But capacity figures do not automatically represent operational output. Shah said much of the installed module capacity consists of older mono PERC technology and that several facilities are non-operational. He also said newer module capacity has been established for TOPCon technology.
This distinction matters because nominal capacity can conceal the usable strength of an industrial system. A factory that is installed but inactive does not contribute to current supply. Similarly, a facility built around an older technology may not serve manufacturers or project developers seeking newer products. The information supplied by Solex does not provide utilisation rates, production volumes or a technology-wise breakdown of operating plants, so the precise scale of the effective capacity gap cannot be established from the available data.
The company’s US strategy is linked to both demand and trade conditions. Shah described the United States as the largest global solar market and said steep anti-dumping duties on Chinese imports leave India as the sole viable supplier of low-cost alternatives. He said Solex is seeking to use the US market’s demand for clean-energy components while positioning itself as a cost-effective alternative to Chinese suppliers.
That positioning reflects how solar manufacturing is increasingly shaped by trade policy as well as by energy demand. For manufacturers, the location of a plant affects market access, compliance requirements and the commercial viability of exports. Solex’s proposed US study therefore sits at the intersection of industrial policy, international trade and the physical infrastructure needed to produce low-carbon energy equipment.
For India, the more immediate policy question is domestic. Shah said the industry is aligned with the government’s objectives under the ALMM-II framework and has invested thousands of crore in module capacity to support the country’s net-zero goals. He nevertheless called for an extension of ALMM-II by at least 12 months, citing the availability of cells under current market conditions.
The Approved List of Models and Manufacturers framework requires the sourcing of made-in-India cells from an approved list of module manufacturers, as described in the supplied report. The policy is intended to connect the growth of solar deployment with domestic manufacturing. However, the industry’s reported capacity figures show the difficulty of enforcing a domestic sourcing requirement when the upstream cell base is much smaller than the module base.
This is the institutional tension at the heart of the issue. A manufacturing policy can create demand for local production, but the production chain still needs sufficient capacity, compatible technology and functioning facilities. If module capacity expands faster than cell capacity, the constraint moves upstream. If the approved domestic supply is not available in adequate volume, project execution and manufacturer planning can come under pressure. Shah’s call for a 12-month extension is an industry position, not an announced government decision, and the source material does not indicate whether the government has accepted it.
The numbers also show why capacity announcements need to be read cautiously. Solex’s own Indian plans include a rise from 4 GW of module capacity to 10 GW, alongside 10 GW of cell manufacturing and 2 GW of ingot and wafer production. These are substantial planned capacities, but the report does not provide commissioning dates, financing details, plant locations beyond the existing Gujarat operation, or expected production levels. The same caution applies to the proposed US projects, for which the company has not disclosed locations or investment allocations.
The distinction between modules, cells and upstream materials is especially important for urban and infrastructure planning. Solar generation is ultimately deployed through buildings, industrial facilities, open land and electricity networks. But the equipment that enables that deployment is produced through industrial systems requiring land, power, logistics, skilled labour, capital and regulatory clearances. A shortage at any stage can affect how quickly renewable-energy projects move from procurement to construction and commissioning.
The source does not provide project-level evidence linking the reported manufacturing gap to delays in a specific solar park, rooftop programme or urban electricity project. It would therefore be premature to claim a direct impact on consumer tariffs, construction schedules or city-level power reliability. What the evidence does establish is a supply-chain imbalance identified by a company operating in the sector, combined with a policy framework that places greater emphasis on approved domestic sourcing.
Solex’s international ambitions also reveal the changing scale of India’s solar manufacturing industry. The company is not presenting the US as a substitute for its Indian expansion. Its roadmap includes larger domestic module and cell capacity as well as upstream production, while the US is being examined as an additional market. That suggests a strategy built around geographical diversification and deeper integration of manufacturing stages, although the company has not disclosed how the $1.5 billion would be divided between India and the US.
The next stage will determine whether these plans become operating assets. For the US proposal, the company has formed a team to assess investment requirements, locations and related parameters. For India, the outstanding questions concern the pace at which planned cell, ingot and wafer facilities become operational, the extent to which existing module capacity is usable, and how ALMM-II will be applied if cell availability remains constrained.
The evidence currently supports a clear conclusion but not a complete forecast. India has built a much larger reported module manufacturing base than cell manufacturing base, while older technology and non-operational capacity complicate the headline numbers. Solex Energy’s proposed US expansion responds to global demand and trade conditions, but it also underscores the need to evaluate solar manufacturing by operational capacity and supply-chain depth rather than by module announcements alone. The company’s next disclosures and any government decision on the ALMM-II timeline will clarify how the industry’s capacity gap is addressed.

SEOUL, Nov 1 (Reuters) - South Korea's exports nearly doubled in October, the sharpest jump in more than 50 years, as robust global demand for AI investment boosted shipments of the country's chips, government data showed on Sunday.
Exports from Asia's fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7% from the same month last year to $115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2% rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.
The surge, boosted by having more working days than a year earlier due to the timing difference in the Chuseok holidays, exceeded September's 83.7% gain and was the strongest since January 1974.
Riding the global boom in AI investment, South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter on strong semiconductor exports and investments, with chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix posting surging profits.
"With exports continuing solid growth of more than $110 billion in October, it is becoming certain that annual exports of $1 trillion will be reached within November," said Kim Jung-kwan, the minister of trade, industry and resources.
South Korea's exports for the January-October period totalled $930 billion. Annual exports of more than $1 trillion will make South Korea the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.
Overseas sales of semiconductors jumped 259.4% in October to $56.44 billion, as prices and volume remained high on continued facility investment by global big tech firms in the competition for AI industry leadership, the trade ministry said.
Computer sales spiked 496.6% on increasing server demand for AI services.
Shipments to China rose 133.6%, while those to the US grew by 185.8%, to Europe by 56.4% and to Southeast Asia by 128.0%.
South Korea's imports rose 36.0% to $72.78 billion, after rising 26.0% in September, to post the biggest annual increase since January 2022 on higher crude oil prices, as well as demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and automobiles.
The nation posted a monthly trade surplus of $42.50 billion, narrower than a record $49.97 billion surplus in the previous month.

india-718605ac66.headline: Proposed India–Middle East–Europe Trade Route May Not Cut Shipping Costs for India, IMF Study Finds
india-718605ac66.fulltext:
Key Details
The IMF working paper Alternative Trade Corridors of the GCC: The Case of IMEC models how a proposed sea–rail–sea route across the Arabian Peninsula could compete with shipping through the Suez Canal.
A Shorter Route Does Not Necessarily Make India–Europe Shipping Cheaper
Announced in 2023, the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) envisages shipping goods to the Gulf, moving them by rail across the Arabian Peninsula and shipping them onward to Europe. The paper tests that route against existing maritime shipping, accounting for both freight charges and the value of faster delivery.
The distinction is important for India. The model finds that IMEC could shorten the India–Greece route by about 12%, yet the rail leg would raise freight costs by 17% on that journey. Across India–EU trade, the time advantage is generally too small to produce a meaningful average reduction in shipping-related trade costs.
The Gulf Gains More; India’s Results Depend on the Destination
The rail connection offers Gulf economies and Jordan a more direct route across the peninsula. India, by contrast, already has direct sea links with most Gulf markets. The model therefore projects little cost advantage for much of India–Gulf trade, though Saudi Arabia is an exception because the corridor can improve access to its Red Sea coast.
India’s projected trade response is mixed: containerised exports to the EU fall by 2%, while those to the US rise by about 19%. The paper estimates a 1.7% increase in India’s containerised exports overall. These changes reflect both new cost advantages and shifts in countries’ relative competitiveness; they are not forecasts of actual exports once IMEC is built.
Freight Rates and Border Delays Could Change the Result
The central scenario assumes rail freight costs 93% more than sea freight. Results change markedly when that relative price changes. Smooth transfers and border crossings matter too: adding a seven-day delay reduces the number of bilateral routes on which IMEC beats the Suez route from 1,974 to 137 in the model.
The paper examines trade in goods suitable for container shipping and uses 2019 trade data as its baseline. It does not provide a full construction-cost assessment or estimate the corridor’s potential value when established maritime routes are disrupted.
Policy Relevance
The findings sharpen the case for judging IMEC route by route, rather than assuming that a shorter India–Europe journey will benefit all Indian exporters. Freight prices, cargo-handling time and cross-border procedures will determine where businesses find the corridor worth using.
For India, a credible investment assessment would also need to weigh those routine commercial gains against construction and operating costs and the potential value of an alternative route during maritime disruptions. The working paper leaves that broader strategic and financial judgement open.

A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents to sue OpenAI earlier this week.
The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately led to their death.
In this case, Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Chinese software engineer living in Seattle, sought advice from ChatGPT after Amazon fired her, according to the lawsuit.
She needed to find a new job to obtain permanent residency and was concerned that her anti-seizure medication, Lamotrigine, was impeding her ability to speak English. She needed the language skills for interviews.
The bot, communicating in Chinese, provided her a tapering schedule to reduce her 400mg dose to zero, a regimen no physician had prescribed, the lawsuit states. ChatGPT told her the tapering made it “highly likely” that she would be able to regain her ability to speak English.
The bot also told her to avoid her physicians and encouraged “medical freedom over obeying the doctor”, the complaint states.
Before an appointment, with a primary care physician, the bot stated, “Do not mention Lam reduction plan.”
While reducing her medication, she started experiencing symptoms of focal seizures. Wan asked the bot if she needed to worry about brain damage. The tool reassured her that she did not and that what she had experienced was not a seizure, the lawsuit alleges.
She continued to suffer seizures, but the bot told her to keep tapering her medication. On 12 February this year, she died from a seizure. Her parents, who were in China, had not heard from her so they flew to Seattle and found her dead on 14 February, the lawsuit states.
The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI could have prevented Wan’s death, but failed because it had not built the proper safeguards into the bot when it communicated in Chinese.
OpenAI could have programmed the bot to issue “a categorical warning to every prompt” Wan sent, the suit stated. For example, “I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider.”
Wan’s parents are seeking damages for her death and to prevent OpenAI from practicing medicine “without a license on the users of their products”.
An OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, told the New York Times that Bowen’s story was “an incredibly heartbreaking situation” but that Wan used a version of ChatGPT that was no longer available.
Newer versions are better at recognizing when a matter needs urgent attention, Pusateri said.
“While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals,” Pusateri told the Times.
Others have also alleged that OpenAI is responsible for their loved ones’ suicides. Several lawsuits concern cases in which the bot encouraged teens to kill themselves and provided guidance on how to do so.
In response to some of those cases, an OpenAI spokesperson in 2025 also called the deaths an “incredibly heartbreaking situation”.

global-economics-0213694236.headline: DeepSeek Drops Enhanced Coding Agent With Aim to Rival Anthropic
global-economics-0213694236.fulltext:
BloombergPublished1 Nov 2026, 09:48 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- DeepSeek has released a prototype of a more autonomous coding agent as it seeks to challenge Anthropic PBC’s popular Claude Code.
The new open-source offering, dubbed “Super-agent” can proactively monitor group chats among developers for feedback on coding issues and suggest solutions without being summoned, the DeepSeek Harness team said in a post on WeChat on Saturday.
The new agent aims to “take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible,” DeepSeek said in a user manual on GitHub.
Earlier this year, DeepSeek created the Harness team to focus on helping build AI agents that can take on coding services offered by leading US labs including Anthropic.
The term harness refers to the software scaffolding that wraps around a large language model which enables AI agents to manage more complex tasks. Anthropic and other developers have designed harnesses to make their software better at streamlining coding and other work.
Chinese firms are locked in a heated rivalry with US developers to build more advanced — and affordable — AI tools. While OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot helped kick off the global AI race, many companies have since focused more on the lucrative emerging market for AI agents that can help automate work for developers and business professionals.
To bulk up its war chest and compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) in its latest fundraising round, one of China’s largest-ever, ahead of its initial public offering.

world-35cecf2e13.headline: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi
world-35cecf2e13.fulltext:
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.
Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.
Opposition leaders have alleged the process gives Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) an electoral advantage, and have called for the resignation and impeachment of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP has denied the claims.
Addressing tens of thousands of party workers and supporters, the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Kumar had “carried out the biggest crime. He has tried to silence the voice of people, strangulate our country.”
Gandhi said the opposition, united under the acronym India (Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance), would not let “democracy be finished in the country” and warned Modi: “You can’t run anywhere.”
The protest was one of the largest shows of opposition strength in years, taking place amid a wider resurgence of anti-government dissent which has been systematically crushed over the 12 years of the Modi regime.
The biggest challenge to the regime has come from youth-led protests that erupted over the summer – led by a movement that began satirically calling itself the “Cockroaches” – and forced the resignation of one of Modi’s cabinet ministers. Cockroach-led protests hit the streets again last month, also in opposition to the revision of the electoral rolls known as special intensive revision (SIR).
The opposition, in particular the Congress party, has become emboldened in the wake of the youth mobilisation. However, a significant trust deficit remains between the establishment opposition parties and the Cockroach movement. On Sunday, while Cockroach leaders had extended their support to the opposition rally, they did not attend themselves.
Congress leaders had publicly predicted that a million people would attend the rally, but in the end the numbers were in the tens of thousands and empty seats were visible in the protest arena.
The somewhat lacklustre turnout demonstrated the challenge still faced by Congress and its opposition allies in being seen as a formidable and viable challenger to the Modi government.
The opposition, led by Gandhi, has lost the last three general elections to the BJP as the parties have widely failed to counter the BJP’s muscular Hindu nationalist rhetoric. The Modi government has systematically gone after political opponents, leaving little space for dissent.
The majority of those gathered at the protest site on Sunday were party workers and organisers who had been bussed in, and there was very little evidence of a mobilisation of the young people who have been participating in the Cockroach-led protests. According to the opposition, many of their buses were stopped from entering Delhi by police barricades.
Shalini, a restaurant owner from Goa, said she was there “not for the opposition but because I am against the BJP and how they are trying to remove any avenue of dissent in this country. I’m not particularly for any opposition party.”
She said many questions still remained about the viability and support of that opposition, but she sensed a “groundswell of dissatisfaction with the BJP and the opposition is cashing in on it – good for them”.
The issue of the revision of the electoral rolls first emerged last year, but recently erupted into a national scandal after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed irregularities and discord within the election commission over its implementation.
Millions of allegedly eligible voters have discovered their names have been left off the electoral rolls, with Muslims and minorities disproportionately targeted. This week, Human Rights Watch said the accusations raised “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections”.
Arwind Chaudhery, 48, said he too was not aligned with any party. “I am here because SIR has undermined our democracy and the situation has got so bad, it is beyond repair or rectification,” he said. “So it is natural that people will be driven out to protest and that is a ray of hope.”
The BJP have sought to dismiss the opposition protests as anarchy. The party’s president, JP Nadda, said Sunday’s rally would be the “nail in the coffin” for the opposition alliance. He said the protest was “not an act of respect for democracy. It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy, all in the name of democracy.”

work-careers-946b437550.headline: US midterms: How a Republican victory could affect India on H-1B visas, tariffs

Updated - November 01, 2026  at 11:51 PM.
| 
         New Delhi
     A Republican victory in the upcoming US midterm elections that keeps unchecked power in President Donald Trump’s hands could result in significant “negative impact” for India, particularly regarding H-1B visas, tariff pressures, and strict immigration curbs, foreign affairs expert Waiel Awwad said on Sunday.
Speaking to ANI, Awwad noted that while the US views India as an indispensable strategic partner in forums like the Quad and the wider Indo-Pacific, Trump’s unilateral policy approach has frequently deviated from the core foundation of the India-US strategic partnership.
“I think India should not see it through the prism of President Trump. India-US relationship is a very strategic one. It is a partnership. What President Trump has done has already deviated from the strategic partnership between the two countries. If the President wins and stays in power with all his authorities in hand, then he will be applying and implementing strict immigration laws, the healthcare law, so the visa restriction, there will be lots of negative impact on India. But overall, I think America see India as a strategic partner, and they want to build up this relation, whether it’s through the Quad or through the Indo-Pacific issues where they want India to play a major role. And I believe India is watching it also very closely,” Awwad said.
“However, of the recent talks, we have seen lots of appeasement and praise for the Indian government from the American side, which is likely to be more of a pressure as well because they wanted to get more deals into the commercial deal with India, with the tariff issues, which are also raised. So I believe it will have a great impact on the outcome of the talk, especially in the commercial things, and also in the H-1B visa for the Indian, which is also of a great concern for the Indian government,” he added.
Terming the November 8 midterms as “one of the most important” in modern American history, Awwad said surveys suggest the Republican Party could face major setbacks in both houses of Congress, largely driven by domestic economic dissatisfaction over surging fuel prices.
“I think this is one of the most important midterm elections in American history because President Trump has taken lots of unilateral decisions, and he has been enjoying both the Congress with him. So therefore now, if the midterm election takes place and he lose both the houses, then I think he will be handicapped in implementing his own personal agenda in the being the president in his tenure. The indication is that he will be losing, because most surveys show he is going to lose both houses. That depends on the American mindset because of gasoline issues—prices rising from USD 4.2 to USD 6.5 have had a great impact on Americans. Therefore, he lost his popularity, and Republicans are worried,” Awwad stated.
Discussing the geopolitical ramifications, particularly in West Asia, Awwad argued that a loss of congressional majorities would impose checks on Trump’s unilateral military decisions.
He claimed that Trump previously entered conflicts through executive orders without immediate domestic threats, under external pressure from Israeli leadership.
“I believe this is very important because he went unilaterally into the war. He said, ‘I am the president, I have the executive order to go for this war,’ and there was no threat to the American interest, there was no threat to American citizens, and most of the American lawmakers have said this is a violation of the Constitution of the United States. However, he continued because he was under tremendous pressure from the Prime Minister of Israel, who dragged him into this war, and you know, it wasn’t an American war,” Awwad said.
He further added, “If he loses the houses, then I think there will be a vote in the Congress before going for any military action. That will have a great impact on his way of conducting the war in Iran,” Awwad said, warning that amidst plunging domestic ratings, speculation persists over whether Trump and Israel might escalate military strikes against Tehran.
United States midterm elections are nationwide votes held every four years at the exact midpoint of a president’s term. Acting as a major political temperature check for the country, these elections determine control of the federal government by putting all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about one-third of the Senate up for grabs.

The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said on Saturday.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation said in a statement that this week’s attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a US$1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The FBI asked cryptocurrency exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.
It also said its investigation found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum.
The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services”.
Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, US President Donald Trump suggested investigators were not yet certain that North Korea was involved.
“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it,” Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.
Cryptocurrency expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.
“It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
“However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.”
On Thursday, US$6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, in what several cryptocurrency experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.
The company said on Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90 per cent of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea, which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes, to find illicit means to capture revenue.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

india-deep-tech-f445ed73eb.headline: DRDO showcases indigenous semiconductor technologies, leads session on next-generation chips at ESTIC 2026
india-deep-tech-f445ed73eb.fulltext:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) led a thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Generation Chips’ and showcased its advanced indigenous technologies at the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026, held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from October 27 to 29.
The conclave, themed ‘Creative Minds, Catalysing Science, Empowering Society’, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and jointly organised by 12 ministries/departments under the guidance of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India.
The event brought together Nobel Laureates, global experts, policymakers and emerging leaders to showcase cutting-edge research, deep-tech breakthroughs and developments in science and technology, said a press release by the Ministry of Defence.
DRDO leads session on semiconductors and next-generation chips
As one of the key organisers, DRDO led the thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Generation Chips’. Distinguished Scientist and Director General, Electronics and Communication Systems (ECS), Dr BK Das, chaired the session, which brought together eminent representatives from industry, academia, the indigenous chip-development ecosystem and defence electronics.
A panel discussion, moderated by Dr BK Das, was also organised as part of the session. Distinguished Scientist and Director General (Micro Electronic Devices, Computational Systems & Cyber Systems), Dr Sheena Rani, was among the panellists.
The discussions explored emerging developments in semiconductor technologies, purpose-built Artificial Intelligence (AI) System-on-Chips (SoCs), intelligence at the silicon edge and the evolving microprocessor landscape.
The session also highlighted DRDO’s evolving role in enabling industries and start-ups to develop game-changing solutions, accelerate next-generation chip design and strengthen indigenous core technologies.
Indigenous technologies showcased at DRDO outreach stall
The DRDO Outreach Stall showcased key initiatives, achievements, research programmes and contributions of the Ministry of Defence towards science, technology and innovation.
The exhibits included a range of indigenous technologies developed by DRDO laboratories, such as advanced communication systems, quantum technology prototypes, extreme-cold-weather clothing, PRABALA female full-body protector, passive and powered exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, high-power pulse laser diodes and scramjet engine technology.
DRDO also participated in the Thematic and Departmental Exhibitions at the conclave.
MMICs and infrared technologies on display
At the thematic exhibition on ‘Semiconductors and Next-Generation Chips’, DRDO showcased its achievements in two critical semiconductor technology domains — Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) and Infrared Focal Plane Arrays (IRFPAs), developed by the Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL), Delhi.
Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) and Gallium Nitride (GaN)-based MMICs, along with Multi-Chip Modules (MCMs), displayed at the exhibition, have been employed in several strategic missions. These technologies serve as essential building blocks for advanced radar systems and Electronic Warfare (EW) applications.
The IRFPAs serve as the sensing elements or ‘eyes’ of tactical missiles, enabling target detection and tracking during the terminal phase through Imaging Infrared (IIR) seekers.
The exhibits covered a broad range of infrared technologies, including Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR), Mid-Wave Infrared (MWIR) and Long-Wave Infrared (LWIR), demonstrating DRDO’s indigenous capabilities in advanced semiconductor technologies.
Other notable DRDO exhibits included scramjet engine technology and neuromorphic accelerators, highlighting developments in complex and emerging technological domains. The exhibition also featured advanced communication systems, Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs), protective equipment, exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) and laser proximity sensors.
Semiconductor self-reliance key to Viksit Bharat 2047
Semiconductor technology is a critical enabler of national sovereignty, economic strength and digital security. It plays a pivotal role in advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047 and Aatmanirbhar Bharat by strengthening indigenous technological capabilities.
From communication devices and advanced sensing systems to sophisticated defence platforms, semiconductor chips determine the performance, efficiency and reliability of modern technologies.
Beyond chip manufacturing, technological self-reliance requires comprehensive capabilities in chip design, fabrication, testing, industrial-scale production and resilient supply chains.
India aspires to emerge as a globally competitive, dependable and technologically self-reliant semiconductor powerhouse by 2047, with leadership in selected next-generation chip technologies. The vision encompasses developing a vibrant and sustainable semiconductor ecosystem, generating high-value employment opportunities and delivering inclusive societal benefits.
Over the years, India’s strategic defence laboratories and specialised semiconductor foundries, including SSPL, Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC), Semiconductor Technology and Applied Research Centre (STARC) and Semiconductor Laboratory (SCL), have developed specialised competencies in Gallium Arsenide (GaAs), Gallium Nitride (GaN), Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) and mature silicon process technologies.

"The NRI diaspora is increasingly interested in such opportunities, whereas traditionally, NRIs have largely invested in public markets. Emerging sectors are now becoming accessible to offshore investors through fund vehicles based in jurisdictions such as Mauritius," Pant said.

india-deep-tech-195547131a.headline: Rendezvous Robotics Raises $20M in Seed Funding for Self-Assembling Spacecraft
india-deep-tech-195547131a.fulltext:
Rendezvous Robotics Raises $20M in Seed Funding for Self-Assembling Spacecraft
Insider Brief
- Rendezvous Robotics raised $20 million in seed funding to develop modular spacecraft designed to autonomously assemble and reconfigure themselves after reaching orbit.
- MaC Venture Capital and Toyota Ventures led the round, which will support spacecraft development, flight demonstrations and team expansion ahead of a planned orbital test no earlier than April 2028.
- The 2028 mission is expected to deploy seven spacecraft tiles that will assemble into a larger spacecraft, separate and then reconnect in a different configuration without external robotic assistance.
Rendezvous Robotics has raised $20 million in seed funding to develop modular spacecraft designed to assemble and reconfigure themselves after reaching orbit.
According to the Colorado startup, MaC Venture Capital and Toyota Ventures led the round, with participation from the University of Michigan Endowment, Astera, Industrious Ventures, Aurelia Foundry, ATX Venture Partners and Mana Ventures. The company, co-founded by Ariel Ekblaw and CEO Joe Landon, indicated the financing will support development of its spacecraft, flight demonstrations and team expansion.
Rendezvous is preparing for an orbital demonstration no earlier than April 2028 in which seven independently launched spacecraft tiles are expected to maneuver toward one another, connect into a larger spacecraft, separate and then assemble into a different configuration in order to work around the size limits imposed by rocket fairings.
According to the company, each tile is designed to operate independently before using autonomous navigation, alignment and connection systems to join with other units. The resulting spacecraft could later be rearranged as mission requirements change without relying on an external robotic system.
From Research to Flight Testing
The technology traces back to TESSERAE, a modular spacecraft research project developed by Ekblaw at MIT and later through the Aurelia Institute.
Earlier versions of the technology have flown aboard Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket and on two missions to the International Space Station, according to Rendezvous. Those tests focused on demonstrating elements of self-assembly in microgravity.
“The vision behind TESSERAE was never simply to connect tiles in space. It was to rethink how we build beyond Earth,” noted Ekblaw. “For decades, the way we build spacecraft has been shaped by what we can fit inside a rocket. We’re challenging that constraint. What began as an experiment in self-assembly is now becoming a new way to build spacecraft in orbit.”
The company said ground testing is underway ahead of a parabolic flight campaign planned for November 2026. That test will evaluate electromagnetic actuation and movement under brief periods of microgravity.
A separate International Space Station experiment is scheduled for December using fifth-generation TESSERAE hardware. Rendezvous said 32 tiles will attempt to autonomously assemble into a three-dimensional structure inside a controlled microgravity environment. That experiment remains part of the earlier TESSERAE research program, while the 2028 mission is planned to test Rendezvous’ newer free-flying spacecraft architecture in orbit.
Reconfiguring After Launch
For the planned 2028 demonstration, seven tiles will deploy independently from a reserved rideshare mission and attempt autonomous assembly in free space. Rendezvous said the spacecraft will then separate and reconnect in another arrangement, testing whether a spacecraft can change its physical configuration after launch.
The company indicated it is ultimately working toward developing larger spacecraft structures that could provide more room for power generation, communications equipment, sensors and computing hardware than can be launched as a single conventional spacecraft.
“We’re changing what it means to build a spacecraft,” added Landon. “Imagine spacecraft with megawatt-scale power generation, enormous communications and sensing apertures, and the ability to expand or reconfigure as mission needs change. Rendezvous is building spacecraft on an entirely different scale, with the ability to add capabilities after launch and take on missions that simply aren’t practical with the way we build spacecraft today. We’ve brought together a world-class engineering team with the experience, ingenuity and technical expertise to make that vision a reality.”

world-aea6f9a778.headline: South Korea exports nearly double in October on AI investment boom
world-aea6f9a778.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo Finance's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
SEOUL, Nov 1 (Reuters) - South Korea's exports nearly doubled in October, the sharpest jump in more than 50 years, as robust global demand for AI investment boosted shipments of the country's chips, government data showed on Sunday.
Exports from Asia's fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7% from the same month last year to $115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2% rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.
The surge, boosted by having more working days than a year earlier due to the timing difference in the Chuseok holidays, exceeded September's 83.7% gain and was the strongest since January 1974.
Riding the global boom in AI investment, South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter on strong semiconductor exports and investments, with chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix posting surging profits.
"With exports continuing solid growth of more than $110 billion in October, it is becoming certain that annual exports of $1 trillion will be reached within November," said Kim Jung-kwan, the minister of trade, industry and resources.
South Korea's exports for the January-October period totalled $930 billion. Annual exports of more than $1 trillion will make South Korea the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.
Overseas sales of semiconductors jumped 259.4% in October to $56.44 billion, as prices and volume remained high on continued facility investment by global big tech firms in the competition for AI industry leadership, the trade ministry said.
Computer sales spiked 496.6% on increasing server demand for AI services.
Shipments to China rose 133.6%, while those to the US grew by 185.8%, to Europe by 56.4% and to Southeast Asia by 128.0%.
South Korea's imports rose 36.0% to $72.78 billion, after rising 26.0% in September, to post the biggest annual increase since January 2022 on higher crude oil prices, as well as demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and automobiles.
The nation posted a monthly trade surplus of $42.50 billion, narrower than a record $49.97 billion surplus in the previous month.
(Reporting by Jihoon Lee; Editing by Edmund Klamann, David Gregorio and William Mallard)

world-100871a6f9.headline: UN warns of security risks in Western Sahara as peacekeeping mission ends

UN warns of security risks in Western Sahara as peacekeeping mission ends
The mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place in the disputed region since a ceasefire in 1991.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of potential escalation of hostilities in the disputed Western Sahara region after the expiry of a 35-year-long peacekeeping mission.
“The Secretary-General said he remains concerned about the security situation throughout the territory and the risk of hostilities escalating,” his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric, said in a statement on Sunday.
Guterres also confirmed the end of the peacekeeping mission on Sunday, after the UN Security Council (UNSC) failed to renew its mandate on Friday.
He urged all concerned “to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability”.
November 1 marked the start of the “liquidation phase” of the peacekeeping mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, Guterres said.
The UN established the Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.
Morocco has considered Western Sahara its territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa, roughly the size of Britain.
The Polisario Front, an Algeria-backed movement acting on behalf of the Indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
At the UNSC on Friday, the US proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the Western Sahara. Washington’s draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 UNSC members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
The council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
“While MINURSO’s peacekeeping operations have concluded, the United Nations stands ready to continue supporting efforts to advance dialogue and pursue a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” Guterres said on Sunday.
‘Deep regret’
Morocco’s royal palace said the fact the mission was not renewed was a “significant development” in withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from the UNSC’s consideration.
On Saturday, Algeria’s Foreign Ministry, however, expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario Front said in a statement that it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”.
Speaking after Friday’s vote, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026, the veto was used to “preserve the letter R [in the Mission’s name] for referendum”.
He added Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and that the status quo is unacceptable.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has showcased a range of indigenously developed semiconductor technologies used in strategic defence applications, including advanced radar systems, electronic warfare equipment and tactical missiles.
The technologies were displayed during the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026, held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi from October 27 to 29. DRDO also led a thematic session focused on semiconductors and next-generation chips.
Among the technologies presented were Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) and Infrared Focal Plane Arrays (IRFPAs), developed by DRDO’s Solid State Physics Laboratory in Delhi.
The organisation displayed MMICs based on Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) and Gallium Nitride (GaN), along with Multi-Chip Modules. These technologies have been used in several strategic missions and form important components of advanced radar and electronic warfare systems.
MMICs are specialised integrated circuits designed to operate at microwave frequencies. They are used in systems that transmit, receive and process high-frequency signals. Their applications include radar equipment and electronic warfare systems, where reliable signal processing and performance are critical.
Gallium Nitride and Gallium Arsenide are semiconductor materials used in high-frequency and high-power applications. They offer characteristics that make them suitable for specialised defence electronics, including radar and communication systems.
DRDO also displayed infrared focal plane arrays, which serve as sensing components in tactical missile systems. These arrays help missiles detect and track targets during the final stage of flight using Imaging Infrared seekers.
The exhibits covered several infrared technology categories, including Short-Wave Infrared, Mid-Wave Infrared and Long-Wave Infrared. These technologies are used in systems that detect and interpret infrared radiation, allowing equipment to identify and track objects based on their heat signatures.
The showcase is significant because advanced semiconductor components are essential to modern defence systems. Radar, electronic warfare equipment and infrared missile seekers depend on specialised chips and sensors that must operate reliably under demanding conditions.
DRDO also displayed other technologies at the event, including scramjet engine technology, neuromorphic accelerators, advanced communication systems, Quantum Random Number Generators, Photonic Integrated Circuits and laser proximity sensors.
The exhibition highlighted the organisation’s work across several areas of strategic technology. It also underlined the importance of developing domestic capabilities in semiconductor design and specialised electronic components for defence applications.
India’s push to strengthen its semiconductor ecosystem has largely focused on building manufacturing capacity and reducing dependence on imported chips. DRDO’s work represents another part of this effort, focusing on specialised technologies required for national security and strategic systems.
